title: Moral Superiority Will Make You a Bad Person
author: The Stoic Manual
summary: The Stoic Manual warns that practicing Stoicism can quietly turn into contempt for other people's faults, leaving the practitioner proud of his discipline and harder to trust. The author describes an acquaintance who used others' shortcomings to raise his own standing, and his own early habit of giving advice before understanding anyone's emotions. He argues that a judgmental manner makes honesty feel unsafe, using a doctor lecturing a patient and a parent overreacting to a child's confession as examples, so people simply stop telling you things. A long reading of Shakespeare's Measure for Measure shows Angelo using his reputation for strictness as cover for his own wrongdoing. The remedy is not to drop standards but to ask first whether people understood the stakes, to enjoy their company, and to redirect judgment onto one's own conduct. For leaders, managers and parents, the piece is a reminder that influence depends on whether people can bring you the truth.
points: Stoic practice can curdle into self-righteousness, making a person more alert to others' faults while excusing his own.
A manner that makes honesty feel unsafe reduces the information you receive, as the lecturing doctor and the harsh parent both discover.
Labeling someone permanently as bad makes change feel pointless and can turn shame into defiance.
Angelo in Measure for Measure shows how attachment to being seen as good leads to defending an image instead of examining oneself.
High standards and honest correction still matter, but they work best after listening, clarifying expectations and offering help.
quotes: Practicing Stoicism can make us more aware of other people’s faults while giving us sensible rationalizations for our own. We become proud of our discipline, impatient with their emotions, and convinced that our harshness is helping.
At first, practicing Stoicism made this worse because it became easy to see people’s pitfalls. Before understanding someone’s emotions, I was giving them advice.
A manner that makes honesty feel unsafe works against the very purpose of asking.
If every failure confirms that someone is the bad person we’ve already decided they are, they may grow tired of trying to prove otherwise. Shame becomes exhausting; defiance offers relief.
That’s the danger of becoming attached to the idea that you’re a good person. You can grow more concerned with defending that identity than examining and dealing with the reality of who you are.

Ostracize someone, make every encounter a judgment of their character, and you may lose opportunities to reach them. That’s why sometimes enjoying their company, taking an interest in what absorbs them, and having fun together makes a difficult conversation possible later.

But imagine looking at your actions, reflecting, making reparations, and doing better for a year. Imagine how much could change if noticing your faults reliably led to a bonding conversation, an apology, or a different choice and habit.
Of course, you still need to recognize wrongdoing, uphold high standards, and tell people the truth, even when they’d rather avoid it. Kindness requires enough courage to have that conversation.
